title: ICE at the Gate: Why Immigration Lawyers Want Every Indian in the US Carrying Documents
excerpt: A new TSA-ICE data-sharing agreement and a wave of airport arrests have sharpened a message immigration attorneys have been repeating for months: carry your papers everywhere, even on domestic flights.
body:
• ICE has arrested at least 27 travelers at US airports for alleged visa overstays, using a newly disclosed TSA data-sharing agreement to identify targets at check-in counters and boarding gates.
  • US Customs and Border Protection issued a public reminder that all non-citizens must carry alien registration documents at all times or face misdemeanor charges and fines.
  • Immigration attorneys recommend Indian nationals on H-1B, F-1, and green cards carry a folder of current status documents even for domestic travel, and consult legal counsel before any international trip.
  • The visa interview waiver window has been cut from 48 months to 12 months, meaning more travelers returning from India now face full consular interviews and risk lengthy administrative processing delays.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have begun pulling passengers off domestic flights inside US airports, marking a sharp escalation in the Trump administration's push to hit a daily target of 2,000 immigration arrests. At least 27 people have been detained for allegedly overstaying their visas, according to reports from The New York Times and ABC News, and immigration attorneys say some of those swept up held valid work authorization and had no criminal history.

The tactic drew national attention in mid-July after a viral video from Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas showed a handcuffed man on the ground surrounded by plainclothes ICE agents. The Department of Homeland Security identified him as an undocumented immigrant from Australia, but the incident rattled travelers of all backgrounds — and it has hit the Indian diaspora, one of the largest non-citizen populations in the United States, with particular force.

How TSA Data Became an Enforcement Tool

On July 28, watchdog group American Oversight published a previously undisclosed memorandum of agreement between the Transportation Security Administration and ICE that outlines how the two agencies share passenger information and how that data is stored and used. Immigration attorney Rosanna Berardi told ABC News that ICE is now "working with TSA and targeting people at check-in counters and gates, sidestepping the warrants and surveillance operations used in the past."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RuPOfTvQr54

"There is no investigation or no home visit involved," Berardi said. "It's simply a name match at a checkpoint, and that's what makes this approach so efficient for ICE and so unsettling for travelers."

"Americans provide their personal information to board a plane safely, not to become part of an immigration enforcement system or a government surveillance network."

— Chioma Chukwu, Executive Director, American Oversight

CBP's Blunt Warning: Carry Your Papers

US Customs and Border Protection posted the message directly on X: "Always carry your alien registration documentation. Not having these when stopped by federal law enforcement can lead to a misdemeanor and fines." The agency cited Section 264(e) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which makes failure to carry valid registration documents a federal misdemeanor.

The warning arrives alongside comments from Vice President JD Vance that have amplified anxiety among Indian immigrants. "A green card does not give an individual an indefinite right to stay in the United States," Vance said, fueling questions about the security of permanent residency itself. Green card holders returning from trips abroad are facing longer secondary inspections at ports of entry, with CBP officers questioning whether they still intend to live in the United States.

What H-1B, F-1, and Green Card Holders Should Do

Immigration attorneys have outlined a practical checklist. H-1B workers should carry their I-797 approval notice, recent pay stubs, an employment verification letter, and their attorney's contact information. F-1 students need a current I-20, recent transcripts, proof of funding, and a valid travel signature. Green card holders should keep evidence of US ties — tax returns, mortgage or lease documents, and family connections — readily accessible.

The visa interview waiver window, known as the "dropbox" process, has been cut from 48 to 12 months. Anyone whose previous visa expired more than a year ago must now schedule a full consular interview in India, and consulates are reporting heavier demand for slots. Administrative processing — the security review that follows some interviews — can last weeks or months, stranding travelers abroad and disrupting jobs, academic terms, and family obligations.

What's Next

The airport arrests signal that immigration enforcement is extending into everyday public spaces that most travelers had considered routine. With ICE under pressure to increase arrest numbers and the TSA-ICE memorandum now under congressional and public scrutiny, airports may become one of the most visible fronts in the administration's broader immigration strategy. Immigration lawyers across the country are delivering the same advice: carry your documents everywhere, answer questions calmly and factually, and never discuss your immigration status without counsel present.
